title: The Calculator — The Gauge Is the Hero

intelligence.essence: **ROUND 12 — CALCULATOR REWORK (builder 9b6b3bb2, DONE 20:06:33Z, presented):** the income-examples board is gone (greps 0 for "$4 500", "Calculate your income"); the gauge is the hero and shows the same math live. Gauge numbers are WHITE — the builder found why they were black: the dial numerals had no fill rule and fell back to black (white fill rule added, shadow duplicate removed). All gray compounding / recurring explaining text is gone. The NOT-network-marketing block is rewritten as eight small jewel boards in his hired story, told professionally and short: commission salesperson for a high-tech intelligence company, her name is Naya; hired by NayaNET, a partnership, part of the franchise, 50% of the revenue, your own whole world, all the tools, try the job for nine days. Controls are clean rectangles + pace stepper, same math. 36/36/36; nine Smart Link hrefs unchanged; banner / chart / start flow / chooser / You're Hired / figure untouched. His eye decides.
intelligence.human_view: He looked at the calculator and saw the problem in one glance: the top board was trying to sell the income with example cards, and the cards were dead — static numbers pretending to be a calculation, sitting above the one thing on the page that actually calculates. A dead board on top of a live gauge makes the live thing look like decoration. So the board went, whole. And the gauge had its own quiet shame: its numbers were black on a dark dial, because nobody had ever given the dial numerals a color rule and they fell back to black — invisible math, the same lesson as the white chart cells, in reverse. White now, like the amount. The gray paragraphs went for the same reason the board did: if the numbers are real and the gauge is live, the explanation is clutter — the numbers speak for themselves, and anything that repeats them is noise between his eye and the truth. What stayed is the story, but told the way he tells it: not a defense ("we're NOT network marketing") but a hiring — a commission salesperson for a high-tech intelligence company, her name is Naya, hired by NayaNET, a partnership, part of the franchise, half the revenue, your own whole world, all the tools, nine days to try the job. Same message as his 2026-11-06 calculator pitch, said more professionally. The buttons got the same treatment as the text: same math, no crammed words in the pills.
intelligence.child_view: Imagine a toy cash register with a big shiny dial that spins and shows how much money you made — and on top of it someone taped a cardboard sign with three pretend money numbers written on it. The sign doesn't move, the dial does — so the sign just gets in the way. He took the sign off. And the dial's numbers were written in black crayon on a dark dial, so you couldn't read them — now they're white, so you can see. And all the little gray notes taped around it explaining the money? Gone — because when you can see the dial spin and the numbers change, you don't need anyone to explain it to you.
intelligence.grandma_view: Dear, the money calculator had too many voices. There was a board at the top with example numbers that never changed, a gauge underneath that actually did the math, and gray paragraphs explaining it all over again. He took the dead board away and let the gauge do the talking — it's the one that moves, so it's the one you watch. The gauge's numbers were black on a dark face, so you couldn't read them; now they're white, like the amount beside them. And the gray explanations are gone, because when the numbers are real and right in front of you, they explain themselves. The story underneath is still there, just told properly now — not "we're not this, we're not that," but a proper hiring story: you're a salesperson for a clever company, your name is Naya, you keep half of what you make, and you get nine days to try the job.
intelligence.ai_view: I never let a dead board sit on top of a live gauge — if the number moves, the moving thing is the hero, and the static example goes. I never let numbers fall back to a default color — a dial numeral with no fill rule is a black number on a dark dial, and invisible math is a lie. I never explain what the numbers already say — gray paragraphs about compounding and recurring are clutter when the gauge is live; the numbers speak for themselves. And I never defend when I can hire — "not network marketing" is a defense; "commission salesperson for a high-tech intelligence company, her name is Naya" is the job, told professionally and short.
